appraisal_events.evidence: « Et il fit à sa mère les reproches que sans doute il se sentait peut-être mériter ; c’est ainsi que les égoïstes ont toujours le dernier mot […] leur propre dureté peut aller jusqu’à la plus extrême cruauté sans que cela fasse à leurs yeux qu’aggraver d’autant la culpabilité de l’être assez indélicat pour souffrir, pour avoir raison »
appraisal_events.explanation: The maxim on egoists is bound to Robert's act by "c'est ainsi", so the narrator's generalization functions as a direct, endorsed condemnation of him: he reproaches the mother he has wronged and turns her suffering into her guilt. The passage nonetheless grants that this egoism wins the exchange — he keeps his resolve and has the last word.

appraisal_events.evidence: « d’elle-même Mme de Marsantes cessa d’insister, car elle sentait qu’elle ne le retiendrait plus » ; « par pitié pour elle » ; « les mères sont très égoïstes […] pour lui dire que je ne lui en veux pas, que je trouve qu’il a eu raison »
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme de Marsantes capitulates completely: she abandons her appeal, takes the charge of egoism onto herself, and wants only to absolve the son who has hurt her, ending by peering down the staircase after him. The narrator's explicit pity and his maxim's concession that the sufferer "a raison" make this defeat sympathetic rather than ridiculous, so the movement is a loss of leverage coupled with a gain in narrator-endorsed esteem.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator's analysis, prompted directly by Robert's reproaches, casts him as a self-justifying egoist capable of cruelty toward his mother, sharply lowering how he is locally appraised.
Within the scene the egoist prevails: Robert keeps his freedom, leaves on his own terms, issues instructions about the narrator's visit, and his mother ends by declaring him in the right.
She loses every hold on her son — she stops insisting because she feels she can no longer keep him, blames herself for his pain, and wants to run after him only to tell him he was right.

Her self-accusation is framed against a maxim that has just assigned the egoism to her son, and the narrator states he would excuse Robert's conduct out of pity for her, so the passage raises her moral standing even as it stages her defeat.

ambiguities: Mme de Marsantes's « les mères sont très égoïstes » can be read either as narrator-endorsed maternal generosity (the reading taken here, supported by the preceding maxim and by his stated pity) or as one more symptom of her capitulation; this materially changes whether her general appraisal rises or falls.
